text.p: The following are some of the leading stories in Finnish papers this morning.
HELSINGIN SANOMAT
- No more budget cuts are planned for 1998, but stringent budget policy will prevail, Prime Minister Paavo Lipponen says.
- Finnish tax authorities have perhaps moved too fast to implement bankruptcy law and companies may start demanding compensation, professor at University of Helsinki says.
- Social Democratic party rejects plans to cut state aid to municipalities.

- Finnish Centre Party, main opposition party, decides stance on European economic and monetary union (EMU) in an extra party conference at end-September. Some party MPs advise members to follow Denmark and Sweden and decide to stay outside EMU.
- Savings banks in late 1980s granted loans to loyal customers at significantly lower interest rates than to others, study on the background of banking crisis shows.
- International tele markets' growth will accelerate to 15 percent annually, says Pekka Tarjanne, secretary general of the U.N. international telecoms organisation ITU.
- Interest in Finnish language and its origins has increased since Finland joined European Union and prepares for presidency in 1999.
KAUPPALEHTI
- Skyrocketing price of Raisio stock has set many of main shareholders selling: for example insurer Tapiola sold about 100,000 shares and made 32 million markka profit.

- Reports in Swedish press of Ericsson taking market share in mobile phones from Nokia should be taken with reservations; sales figures are not fully comparable, says Pekka Ala-Pietila, head of Nokia Mobile Phones.
- Government's stringent budget policy does not great pose threats to economic growth and is acceptable, economists say.
- Steel prices will rise significantly towards year-end, steel group Rautaruukki forecasts.
- Trade and industry ministry's proposal to combine state specialised financing institutions in one company has received positive response from sector representatives.
AAMULEHTI
- Old system of price control for rental apartments will not return, says Social and Health Minister Sinikka Monkare.
- State spending could be cut even more than planned, Europe Minister Ole Norrback says.
TURUN SANOMAT
- Increased subscriptions and advertising income prompt Finnish newspapers to forecast two good years ahead, publishing house Sanoma Oy's deputy director Jaakko Rairamo says.
-- Nora Hallberg, Helsinki Newsroom +358-9-680 50 292
